title: The 7 Types of Databases
summary: Compare seven useful database families by the shape of their data, the questions they answer well, and the trade-offs they introduce.
prerequisites: How the Web Works helps explain where a database sits in a system.
learningOutcomes: Choose a starting database from access patterns and guarantees.
Explain when multiple specialized stores are justified.

heroVisual.title: Seven families, seven optimized question shapes
heroVisual.caption: The taxonomy is a practical decision model, not a universal law.

nodes.label: Relational
nodes.detail: Rows, columns, constraints, joins, and transactions.

nodes.label: Document
nodes.detail: Nested records retrieved around an aggregate.

nodes.label: Key–value

nodes.label: Time-series
nodes.detail: Measurements ordered and aggregated over time.

nodes.label: Search engine
nodes.detail: Text and fields ranked by relevance.

sections.title: 1. Start with questions, not product names
sections.summary: A database is chosen to serve access patterns and guarantees, not fashion.

items.title: Name the records
items.explanation: List the facts the system must preserve.
items.result: You can describe the durable data without implementation terms.

items.title: Name the reads
items.explanation: Write the most important questions and their required speed.

items.title: Name the writes
items.explanation: Estimate frequency, concurrency, and conflict behavior.

items.title: Name the guarantees
items.explanation: Decide which operations must be atomic, durable, ordered, or auditable.

items.title: Name the operating limits
items.explanation: Set scale, recovery, latency, cost, team skill, and compliance boundaries.
items.result: The choice reflects the whole system.

blocks.title: “NoSQL” is not one database type
blocks.body: It groups several different data models and trade-offs. Document, key–value, graph, time-series, search, and vector stores should be evaluated separately.

blocks.title: Default responsibly
blocks.body: A relational database is often a strong default for business systems because constraints, transactions, and flexible querying protect evolving data. Move away from the default only for a demonstrated pressure.

sections.title: 2. Relational databases: connected facts with strong rules
sections.summary: Tables and constraints make relationships explicit and enforceable.

visual.title: A relational model
visual.caption: The schema protects meaning before a query runs.

nodes.label: Column
nodes.detail: Defines an attribute and data type.

nodes.label: Transaction
nodes.detail: Commits related changes as one unit.

blocks.text: Relational databases store data in tables and use keys to connect records. SQL expresses selection, joins, aggregation, and change. The database can enforce uniqueness, references, types, and transactional invariants centrally.

blocks.code:
SELECT customer.name, SUM(invoice.total) AS lifetime_value
FROM customer
JOIN invoice ON invoice.customer_id = customer.id
GROUP BY customer.id, customer.name
ORDER BY lifetime_value DESC;
blocks.explanation: A join combines related records while aggregation answers a cross-record business question.

items.title: Use when
items.summary: Correctness spans multiple records, relationships matter, and queries will evolve.
items.whenToUse: Orders, billing, inventory, permissions, clinical or financial records.

items.title: Avoid forcing it
items.summary: A single operation must traverse a massive relationship graph or ingest a specialized signal stream.
items.whenToUse: Keep the relational system as source of truth and add a specialized projection only when measured.

sections.title: 3. Document databases: records shaped like application aggregates
sections.summary: A document keeps related nested data together.

blocks.text: A document database stores self-contained records, commonly represented with JSON-like fields and nested arrays. It fits data that is usually created, retrieved, and changed as one aggregate and whose optional fields vary.

blocks.explanation: The course and its ordered lessons can be loaded together when that is the dominant access pattern.

blocks.title: Flexible schema does not mean no schema
blocks.body: Applications still depend on field meanings, types, required values, migrations, indexes, and validation. The rules may be enforced in different places, but they still exist.

items.title: Use when
items.summary: The aggregate is naturally nested and most reads retrieve it as a whole.
items.whenToUse: Content, product catalogs, profiles, event payloads.

items.title: Avoid when
items.summary: Many independent records must be joined and changed together under strict invariants.
items.whenToUse: Complex financial ledgers or highly connected normalized business data.

sections.title: 4. Key–value databases: the shortest path to a known item
sections.summary: A unique key directly addresses a value.

blocks.text: A key–value database optimizes operations such as get, set, increment, and expire. The database may treat the value as opaque or expose limited data structures. It is excellent when the application already knows the exact key.

blocks.caption: Key design is part of the data model

blocks.title: Caching changes correctness
blocks.body: Define expiration, invalidation, stampede protection, stale behavior, and what happens when the cache is unavailable.

items.title: Use when
items.summary: The primary operation is direct lookup or simple atomic mutation by key.
items.whenToUse: Caching, sessions, counters, queues, ephemeral coordination.

items.title: Avoid when
items.summary: Users need open-ended filtering, joins, or rich ad hoc queries.

sections.title: 5. Graph databases: relationships are first-class data
sections.summary: Graph stores optimize connected paths and neighborhoods.

blocks.text: A graph database models nodes, relationships, and properties. Its strength appears when the number or depth of connections is central to the question, such as shortest paths, recommendations, dependency chains, or fraud rings.

items.title: Use when
items.whenToUse: Social connections, identity graphs, network topology, recommendations.

items.title: Avoid when
items.summary: Data is mostly independent rows with straightforward filters and aggregates.
items.example: A relational database may be simpler

blocks.title: Relational databases can represent graphs
blocks.body: The choice changes when graph traversal is a dominant workload and graph-specific query and storage behavior materially simplify it.

visual.title: Graph question shape
visual.caption: The work follows edges rather than joining many tables repeatedly.

nodes.label: Recommendation
nodes.detail: A result derived from a path.

sections.title: 6. Time-series, search, and vector databases
sections.summary: These stores optimize specialized retrieval rather than general business transactions.

items.title: Time-series
items.summary: Measurements are indexed by time and commonly grouped, downsampled, retained, and queried over windows.
items.avoidWhen: Avoid treating mutable business entities as measurements.
items.example: CPU usage per host per minute

items.title: Search engine
items.summary: Documents and fields are analyzed into an inverted index so terms can be filtered and ranked.
items.avoidWhen: Avoid using a search index as the sole authoritative transaction store.

items.title: Vector
items.summary: Items are encoded as numeric vectors and retrieved by approximate similarity.
items.whenToUse: Semantic retrieval, recommendations, image or text similarity.
items.avoidWhen: Avoid expecting similarity to enforce exact rules or truth.

rows: How did a measurement change over a time window?
Which records match these words and filters, ranked usefully?
Which items are mathematically similar to this item or query?
blocks.caption: Specialized stores are often projections of authoritative data

blocks.title: A vector database does not understand meaning like a person
blocks.body: An embedding model produces coordinates. Similarity finds nearby coordinates; the result can still be irrelevant, outdated, unsafe, or false and must be evaluated.

sections.title: 7. Use more than one database only for proven pressure
sections.summary: Polyglot persistence can improve a system or multiply its failure modes.

items.title: Project intentionally
items.explanation: Copy only the fields needed by the secondary access pattern.
items.result: The projection has a clear contract.

items.title: Define freshness
items.explanation: State whether updates are synchronous, asynchronous, or eventually consistent.
items.result: Users know what delay is acceptable.

items.title: Reconcile failures
items.explanation: Retry idempotently and detect missing or duplicate updates.

items.title: Observe drift
items.explanation: Measure lag, failed events, and mismatched records.

items: A second database solves a measured access-pattern or scale problem.
The team can operate, secure, back up, and restore it.
Data ownership and deletion propagate correctly.
The application defines degraded behavior when it is unavailable.

blocks.title: The simplest durable design wins
blocks.body: One well-modeled database with appropriate indexes is easier to reason about than a distributed collection of stores. Add specialization after evidence, not anticipation.

sections.title: 8. A practical selection matrix
sections.summary: Use this as a starting hypothesis, then validate with representative data and workload.

rows: Embedding quality, recall, filtering, evaluation set.
blocks.caption: First database to evaluate by dominant access pattern

items: Prototype the hardest read and write paths.
Test backup and restore, not only happy-path queries.
Measure p95/p99 latency and resource cost.
Document the rejected alternatives and the evidence.

glossary.definition: A recurring way data is written, selected, filtered, joined, traversed, or aggregated.
A rule the database enforces to reject invalid data states.
An additional data structure that speeds selected lookups at the cost of storage and write work.
A unit of work whose changes are committed or rolled back according to defined guarantees.
A derived representation optimized for a particular read model, search, or analysis need.
